title: Relative pronouns: que, quien, donde, lo que
why: To build richer sentences, the learner links two ideas with que, quien, donde, el que and lo que, compared with English who, which, that, whose and where. This lesson opens the unit on complex sentences and is useful everywhere afterward: describing, specifying, arguing.

{"lessons": ["

Que: “who,” “which” and “that” all at once

In English, you choose between “who” (people), “which” (things) and “that.” In Spanish, it's simpler: one word, que, does it all. It works for people and things, as subject or object.

EnglishSpanish
The girl who works with me is from Toledo.La chica que trabaja conmigo es de Toledo.
The book (that) I'm reading is very good.El libro que leo es muy bueno.
The neighbors who live across the street are lovely.Los vecinos que viven enfrente son encantadores.
The apartment (that) we rent has two bedrooms.El piso que alquilamos tiene dos habitaciones.

Two traps for English speakers. First, translating “who” as quien: right after a noun, with no preposition, it's always que: la mujer que vive arriba, never “la mujer quien vive arriba.” Second, dropping the relative: English can say “the book I'm reading,” but Spanish can never leave the relative out.

The relative que has no accent: the accent is only for questions and exclamations (¿Qué haces?, ¡Qué bonito!).

El que, la que, los que: the one who, the one that

When the noun isn't repeated, you put the article before que. The article agrees with what it replaces:

Mi coche no es este, es el que está al lado.My car isn't this one, it's the one next to it.
Mi hermana es la que lleva gafas.My sister is the one wearing glasses.
Los que viven aquí conocen bien el barrio.Those who live here know the neighborhood well.
", "

After a preposition: con quien, en el que, donde

When the relative follows a preposition (with whom, in which, for which…), the preposition always comes first. English often puts it at the end (“the friend I traveled with”), but Spanish never does.

For…SpanishEnglish
a personla amiga con quien viajé / con la que viajéthe friend I traveled with
peoplelos vecinos con quienes hablo / con los que hablothe neighbors I talk to
a thingla empresa en la que trabajothe company I work for (in which I work)
a placeel barrio donde vivo / en el que vivothe neighborhood where I live

Quien (plural quienes) is only used for people, and here after a preposition. For things, use el que, la que, los que, las que, agreeing with the noun. For a place, donde means “where,” with no accent since it isn't a question.

“About which,” “that I told you about”

When English ends with “about” or “of,” Spanish usually uses de + el que / la que / quien, placed at the front:

Es el compañero del que te hablé.He's the coworker I told you about.
Es la película de la que todo el mundo habla.It's the movie everyone is talking about.

To recognize: cuyo, cuya, cuyos, cuyas means “whose.” Unlike English “whose,” it agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: una amiga cuyo padre es médico (a friend whose father is a doctor), un pueblo cuyas calles son estrechas. It's mostly written; in speech, people prefer other phrasings.

", "

Lo que: “what” (= the thing that)

When “what” or “the thing that” doesn't refer to a specific noun but to an idea, Spanish says lo que. Lo here is a neuter article.

EnglishSpanish
What I want is to rest.Lo que quiero es descansar.
What I like most about Madrid is the atmosphere.Lo que más me gusta de Madrid es el ambiente.
I don't like what you've done.No me gusta lo que has hecho.
Everything you need is in the drawer.Todo lo que necesitas está en el cajón.

Careful: in these sentences, English “what” is not the question word qué (with an accent) but “the thing that”: Lo que quiero es descansar. And todo lo que = everything that, all that.

Don't mix up lo que and el que: el que replaces a masculine noun (mi coche es el que está ahí), lo que an idea (lo que dices es verdad).

which (after a preposition)el que, la que, los que, las que

the one who, the one thatel que, la que
